items.title: Digital Economy and Economic Growth: Productivity Channels, Global Evidence, and Policy Priorities for an Inclusive Digital Transition
items.abstract: The digital economy has become a central component of contemporary economic transformation, but its contribution to growth is neither automatic nor evenly distributed. This article examines the principal channels through which digitalization can influence economic growth and synthesizes recent global evidence on productivity, innovation, employment, human capital, infrastructure, and institutional readiness. The study adopts a structured narrative-review approach drawing on established economic literature, recent peer-reviewed studies, and international policy reports. Three research questions guide the analysis: through which mechanisms does digitalization affect economic growth; why do growth effects differ across countries, firms, and sectors; and which policy conditions are most important for converting digital adoption into inclusive and sustainable economic gains? The review finds that digital technologies can raise productivity by lowering transaction and coordination costs, improving information use, enabling automation, expanding market access, and accelerating innovation. However, recent evidence also shows that productivity effects may be heterogeneous and nonlinear, particularly where firms lack complementary organizational capabilities, skills, finance, or absorptive capacity. Digital infrastructure and broadband remain foundational, while human capital and digital skills determine the extent to which firms and workers can exploit technological opportunities. Artificial intelligence, cloud computing, data analytics, and digital platforms are likely to strengthen these channels but may also intensify labor-market adjustment, market concentration, cybersecurity risks, and digital inequality. The article proposes an integrated policy framework centered on infrastructure, diffusion, skills, innovation capacity, institutional quality, and inclusion. It concludes that digitalization should be understood as a complementary-capabilities process rather than a stand-alone technological shock: long-term growth depends on how effectively digital technologies are combined with human capital, organizational change, competition, and responsive public policy.

items.title: Do LLMs Really Lack Difference Awareness? Uncovering Heuristic Substitution in Group-Differentiating Fairness
items.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the issue of difference awareness in LLMs, defined as a model's ability to recognize and acknowledge meaningful differences between social groups in fairness decision-making. Previous studies have consistently shown that models perform poorly on such tasks, a finding commonly attributed to a lack of difference awareness. We propose an alternative account, which we term Fairness Heuristic Substitution: difference awareness is not necessarily absent, but the complex demand of simultaneously identifying relevant group differences and determining their implications for fairness decisions may lead models to substitute the simpler, more accessible equal-treatment heuristic, i.e., formal equality. Based on this hypothesis, we introduce TDD, a Two-stage Distinguish-Decide framework that explicitly decomposes fairness reasoning into first distinguishing contextually relevant group differences and then making the corresponding decision, thereby discouraging reliance on formal-equality shortcuts. (i) Across four benchmarks and ten models ranging from billions to trillions of parameters, TDD significantly outperforms one-stage baselines, even one strengthened through simulated test-set leakage. (ii) Combining TDD with neuron-level contrastive probing provides mechanistic evidence consistent with the Fairness Heuristic Substitution hypothesis by revealing two signatures of the formal-equality: a compact, locally coordinated representational structure and a pronounced activation bias under default reasoning. (iii) TDD's stage-wise decomposition uncovers overlooked failure modes in fairness reasoning, including heuristic displacement and misaligned stage dynamics.

items.title: Electrodermal activity as a physiological marker of stress and experience-related differences in workers performing work at heights: A real-world functional data analysis study of certified and novice firefighters
items.abstract: Falls from heights remain a leading cause of fatal workplace accidents, with psychological stress contributing to human error. Electrodermal activity (EDA) and heart rate (HR) are promising stress markers whose real-world, physically demanding applicability remains underexplored. This study examined whether EDA and HR discriminate stress responses between certified and basically trained firefighters, and how these responses evolve across task phases. Seventeen male firefighters from the Moravian-Silesian Region, Czech Republic, completed an ascent, tower-top stay, and rappel from a 50-meter industrial cooling tower. EDA was recorded at the wrist and lumbar region using Sensetio wearable sensors, and HR via a Polar H10+ chest strap. After visual inspection, SCL was extracted from EDA; SCL and HR were both resampled to 600 samples (200 per phase) and min–max normalized. Functional data analysis using point-wise Mann–Whitney U tests, complemented by a cluster-based permutation test for multiple comparisons, compared SCL and HR between groups. SCL increased in both groups, but novices showed an earlier, steeper rise during the ascent and tower-top phases, forming two significant clusters after permutation correction ( t ≈ 59 –213, p c l u s t e r = 0.026 ; t ≈ 219 –421, p c l u s t e r = 0.017 ) with large effect sizes (median r = 0.71 ), whereas certified firefighters showed marked increases mainly during rappelling, where the difference narrowed and lost significance (median r = 0.46 ). No significant between-group HR differences emerged. Normalized SCL trajectories thus captured experience-related timing differences that HR did not, suggesting EDA warrants further investigation as a complement to safety training and monitoring, rather than as a validated readiness or error-risk-prediction tool at this stage.

items.title: EMPLOYEE WELL-BEING AND ORGANIZATIONAL PERFORMANCE: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF WORKPLACE INTERVENTIONS AND OUTCOMES
items.abstract: The health and wellness of employees is now a focal point for companies aiming to optimize employee performance, build robust organizational performance, and ensure sustainable results. This systematic review aims to explore the connection between staff wellbeing and organisational performance, focusing on interventions in the workplace, implementation and outcomes. The review draws together the findings of literature on various interventions, such as the mental health support programs, flexible working arrangements, employee assistance programs, occupational health and safety interventions, leadership development, work–life balance policies, and employee involvement in organizational decision making. The results show that interventions at work that emphasize the psychological, physical and social wellness of workers can benefit job satisfaction, employee engagement, productivity, organizational commitment and retention. The review also emphasizes the need for ‘positive organisational culture', supportive leadership, ‘manageable workloads' and psychologically safe working environments to enhance the effectiveness of well-being strategies. But factors including lack of financial support, poor managerial support, stigma, uneven implementation, and measuring long-term effects may reduce their impact. Contextual factors, such as organizational size, industry attributes, employment conditions, and workforce diversity also play a role in the link between employee well-being and organizational performance. The review concludes that the wellbeing of employees should not be seen as a standalone human resource responsibility, but as a part of the strategy of the organisation. It suggests implementing workplace interventions that are evidence-based, based on inclusiveness, and continually assessed, balancing employee needs and organizational goals. The learnings from these insights are valuable in helping to build a broader picture of how employee well-being programs can contribute to sustainable performance and help managers, HR, and organizational policy makers better guide their employees.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has established itself as an engine for change in a variety of disciplines, reinventing operations, making decisions, and processes. AI has incredible potential in education that could enhance educational experiences, optimise administrative processes, and promote personalised education (Sadiku, M. N. et al, 2022). As educational institutions attempt to meet the needs of the digital age, investigating AI applications becomes critical (Pedro, F., et al., 2019). This early inquiry intends to look into the potential uses of AI in management colleges in Jaipur, India. The incorporation of AI into educational institutions has the potential to overcome a number of difficulties that exist in the traditional educational framework. As stated by Rane, N. et al. (2023), AI-powered technology can provide personalised learning experiences tailored to specific student needs, increasing student engagement and boosting learning results. Furthermore, AI-driven analytics can provide useful insights into studentperformance trends, allowing for early intervention measures to address academic issues (Jones et al., 2019). The landscape of AI use in educational institutions is rapidly changing. AI-powered chatbots are being used by institutions around the world to handle administrative activities like admissions, course registrations, and student inquiries (Alvarez, 2018). Furthermore, AI-powered learning management systems (LMS) are being used to provide adaptive learning experiences that dynamically modify content delivery based on student success and personal preferences (Wang et al., 2021)

items.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence in Management Information Systems: From Prediction to Managerial Decision-Making
items.abstract: The use of machine-learning models in management information systems enables organizations to generate predictions at increasing scale and speed. Predictive performance alone, however, is insufficient for managerial use. Decision makers also need to examine why an output was produced, interpret the explanation within the decision context, and monitor the consequences of resulting actions. This chapter treats explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) as an intermediate layer between machine-learning predictions and managerial decision-making. It integrates the literatures on decision support systems, human collaboration with artificial intelligence (AI), and human-centered XAI evaluation. To maintain a focused technical scope, the chapter examines two widely used methods for explaining the outputs of trained models: Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Drawing on the literature reviewed, the chapter develops a four-layer framework that connects prediction, explanation, managerial interpretation and evaluation, and decision, action, and feedback. Published studies from manufacturing, finance and credit, and energy management are then used to examine how these four layers appear in different application settings. The analysis indicates that explanations do not automatically produce trust, decision quality, or ethical acceptability. Their managerial value depends on the joint evaluation of technical properties, user and task characteristics, organizational context, and governance arrangements.

items.title: Explicit Discontinuance and Switching Signals in Generative AI Applications: A Comparative Analysis across Nine Apps
items.abstract: This study examines explicitly reported discontinuance and platform-switching signals in Turkish- and English-language Google Play reviews of nine generative artificial intelligence applications. A total of 1,145,267 reviews posted between 1 July 2025 and 30 June 2026 were screened using rule-based procedures. Of 11,960 candidate reviews, 821 that met strict contextual rules were evaluated in two blind AI-assisted coding passes. The final high-confidence analysis set comprised 692 records, including 543 signals in which discontinuance or switching was reported as having occurred and 149 signals expressing discontinuance intention. To assess the recall limitation of the strict screen, an additional application-by-language stratified sample of 500 reviews was audited from the broader pool of 11,139 records, revealing 110 missed explicit signals. The stratified weighted estimate of the proportion of missed explicit signals in the broad pool was 21.6% (95% CI: 18.2%-25.2%). Accordingly, rates reported per 10,000 reviews are interpreted as high-confidence detection indicators rather than prevalence estimates. Within the high-confidence set, the most frequent reasons were response quality/task failure, technical problems, privacy/trust, and pricing. Among platform switches reported as having occurred, Gemini and Claude were the most frequent destinations. By separating intention from signals of reported enacted behavior and by explicitly reporting screening sensitivity, this study provides complementary evidence to the post-adoption literature on generative AI.

items.title: Fostering self-management competencies through AI-based coaching: mechanisms of inhibition and approach motivation, and intrinsic goal motivation
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based coaching helps individuals attain their goals, yet its effects on self-management and the mechanisms underlying these effects remain poorly understood. Self-management includes self-regulation, self-access, self-control, and volitional facilitation. We hypothesised that the anonymous and nonjudgmental nature of AI-based coaching reduces inhibition and fosters approach motivation, activating intrinsic goal motivation and supporting self-management processes. In a quasi-experimental controlled trial (N = 111), we compared an AI-based coach (chatbot) with a self-coaching intervention (control condition). No significant Condition × Time interactions were observed for the outcome variables. Exploratory pairwise comparisons indicated improvements in self-regulation in both conditions. Within-group patterns suggested increased volitional facilitation following AI-based coaching and increased self-access following self-coaching. No significant effects emerged for self-control. Path analyses revealed that during coaching, chatbot users felt less inhibited and more approach-motivated than self-coaching users, which boosted their motivation to work on their goals and strengthened self-management. The findings suggest that AI-based coaching may foster self-management and that these effects may emerge through motivational processes. Whether the relationship plays a less central role in AI-based coaching than in human coaching remains an open question.

items.title: From Concept to Production
items.abstract: This article examines the potential integration of artificial intelligence tools into the filmmaking process, with a focus on the Pre-Production stage, which includes the design, development, and preparation of production, especially for animated films. Through interviews with experts, literature review, open-source tool testing, and participation in real film projects, the study examines the creative and technical roles that AI can assume during Pre‑Production. The research analyzes how AI technologies influence early production workflows and evaluates their broader impact on the production pipeline through comparative assessments and real‑world applications. Adopting a dual methodological approach that combines a systematic literature review with an applied experimental study, the article moves from a conceptual examination of AI’s capabilities to a collaborative, practice‑based experimental investigation.The first experiment provides a comprehensive review of available AI tools, while the second presents a practical experiment in which students and industry professionals collaborated to create short films using AI‑driven production methods. The study aims to highlight the possibilities, limitations, and challenges arising from AI integration in the pre-production of animated films, contributing to the discussion on the evolution of the film industry and the use of modern technologies in the creative process.

items.title: From Formulation to Articulation: Considerations for AI-Assisted Research in Information Theory
items.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence have contributed to several information-theoretic results through genuinely different modes: a language model may suggest a proof, participate in an extended mathematical dialogue, coordinate computation, or operate as one component of a search harness. Treating all of these as "AI-discovered mathematics" obscures distinctions that matter for scientific reliability, attribution, and reproducibility. This article examines a set of recent cases through a four-stage pipeline: how the problem was formulated; how AI participated in finding a solution; how the resulting analytical and computational claims were verified; and how machine-generated outputs were translated into mathematical exposition for human understanding. Based on these cases, we recommend that research publications (1) disclose the nature and extent of AI assistance at each stage, (2) report verification of analytical reasoning separately from certification of numerical computations, and (3) place more emphasis on articulating the underlying ideas, techniques, and interpretations.

items.title: From Proposal to Execution: Modeling Interaction Semantics in Shared Autonomy
items.abstract: In many human-AI systems, candidate actions are not executed directly but are first evaluated by another decision-making entity under a potentially different objective or decision model. Standard decision-theoretic frameworks do not require this interaction to be represented explicitly, as they define transition dynamics directly over state-action pairs, allowing evaluation to be absorbed within the transition model. We introduce a semantics-aware decision framework in which a candidate action is proposed, evaluated under an interaction context, and then resolved into an executed outcome. We formalize this through a joint action language and an interpretation function that maps each joint action and context to a semantic outcome. Transition and reward dynamics are induced through these semantic outcomes, thereby introducing an explicit representational layer for interaction semantics. Semantic outcomes provide explicit units for organizing interaction principles, which can be instantiated through application-specific evaluation mechanisms and reused across distinct interaction instances. This provides a structured interface for specifying context-dependent evaluation separately from the resulting execution dynamics, without requiring changes to the underlying planning algorithm. We instantiate the framework in shared human-AI autonomy, capturing interaction patterns such as advisory and authorization, and illustrating how interaction context influences decision making. The resulting formulation remains compatible with standard Markov decision process (MDP) planning.

items.title: From the Wiki Incident through Car and Property Metaphors to a Topology of an AI Civilization
items.abstract: Version 1.00 This essay develops a conceptual framework for the emerging infrastructure of an AI civilization, starting from a concrete real-world incident involving AI agents acting on public wikis. Using the metaphors of a traffic accident and of agents entering another party’s digital property, it derives step by step a set of practical requirements: agent identification, a responsibility address, run or session identity, respect for local rules, incident reconstruction, liability, insurance, certification, and shared responsibility across operators, platforms, model providers, and other actors. The essay does not propose a complete regulatory system. Its method is deliberately incremental: introduce only what becomes necessary from the next concrete problem, and allow institutions and standards to evolve from practice. An accompanying appendix maps these ideas to parallel work already under way in research, standardisation, regulation, and industry, including agent identity, delegation, auditability, incident reporting, insurance, certification, and machine-readable website policies. The central proposal is not a new theory of AI governance, but a way of seeing how already emerging pieces may fit into a broader topology of relationships among actors, spaces, permissions, actions, damage, responsibility, and institutions.

items.title: Generative AI in Higher Education: Global Trends, Challenges, and Policy Implications
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has moved from a peripheral tool to a routine feature of student life in higher education.This paper examines how generative AI, and ChatGPT specifically, is used across global and regional student populations, and what challenges accompany that use.Drawing on secondary analysis of four public survey datasets, including a global sample of 23,218 students across 110 countries (Ravšelj et al., 2025) and three available regional datasets from Bangladesh, Colombia, and Ecuador, the study addresses three research questions concerning prevalence and institutional readiness, task level application and regional variation, and the ethical and institutional challenges tied to AI adoption.Results show that 71.4% of the global sample had used ChatGPT, primarily for brainstorming, summarizing, and research assistance, though usage intensity and institutional policy awareness varied meaningfully by region.The three regional datasets converge on a common theme even though each measure it differently: a substantial share of students report reduced verification behavior and self-perceived overreliance on AI tools, a pattern this paper terms experienced dependency to distinguish it from the abstract ethical concern measured by the global dataset.The paper argues that adoption, ethical concern, and experienced dependency function as related but distinct dimensions rather than opposite poles of a single spectrum, and that institutions should track them independently.Implications for policy, faculty development, and future research are discussed.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Marketing: Consumer Responses, Authenticity, and Governance Challenges
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has moved within a few years from experimental tool to routine instrument in marketing departments, and the academic literature is still catching up with that speed. This chapter offers a structured review of work published between 2020 and 2026 on how GenAI is used in marketing, how consumers respond to it, and which governance questions follow. Drawing on journal articles from marketing, information systems, economics and law, together with regulatory documents from the European Union and Türkiye, the chapter first separates predictive from generative systems and maps their uses in content production, personalization, customer interaction and marketing research. It then organizes the consumer evidence around three recurring themes: task-dependent preference for machine advice, authenticity penalties attached to perceived AI authorship, and the ambiguous effects of humanlike design in service encounters. Field and experimental studies of workplace use point to productivity gains that are uneven across workers, while creativity research shows a tension between individual output quality and collective diversity. The chapter also discusses hallucination, representational bias, privacy and dark patterns, the energy demand of large models, and the transparency duties introduced by the EU Artificial Intelligence Act alongside Turkish data protection guidance. Much of the evidence rests on short online experiments and on firms in North America and Europe, so conclusions about long-term behavior and about Türkiye remain provisional. The chapter closes with a research agenda on longitudinal field designs, disclosure formats, cross-cultural replication and the measurement of environmental cost in marketing operations. For managers, the evidence suggests that the source, tone and disclosure of generated content matter as much as its quality.

items.title: HEALTHCARE AI
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored in healthcare to support access to information, patient engagement, administrativeefficiency, and selected clinical workflows. This paper proposes a Healthcare AI framework that organizes healthcare-related requests andprovides structured, understandable information through a digital interface. The framework combines a user interface, request classification,retrieval from approved healthcare information sources, privacy and safety checks, and a response-generation layer. It can support generalhealth education, service navigation, and appointment-related guidance where authorized services are available. The system is designed tocommunicate uncertainty, protect sensitive information, and direct users to qualified professionals when a request is outside its scope. It is notintended to diagnose conditions, prescribe treatment, or replace clinical judgement. The proposed design is modular and can be evaluatedthrough documented software, usability, source-quality, privacy, and safety tests

items.title: How AI developers acquire training data: six channels and the shift away from the open web
items.abstract: Developers of large AI models obtain training data through six channels: collection from the open web without a licence, licences from publishers and platforms, commissioned human and expert work, the purchase or licence of organisations' internal records, purpose-built environments and synthetic data, and data from their own users and devices. This paper describes each channel from a public-record compilation read on 18 October 2026: 122 quantified supply facts, 111 disclosed licensing deals, 83 lawsuits, rulings and regulatory actions, 227 financial records of data vendors, 111 funding events, 110 brokerage records and 1,022 price observations, with a robots.txt census of 6,094 websites. The open web remains the largest source by volume, but access is narrowing: 11.4 percent of the census sites shut at least one AI crawler out of the whole site, and an earlier audit found restrictions on 28 percent or more of the most actively maintained sources of a standard web corpus. Of the 83 legal records, 70 concern content taken without a licence and 12 concern developers' use of their own users' data; none concerns the channels in which developers pay for data. Money is moving to those paid channels: disclosed licences, data vendors whose newest reported revenues or run rates exceed one billion dollars, and, since 2026, published programmes that buy organisations' records. We set out the scale, prices and legal exposure of each channel (not legal advice), the limits of the record, and what the shift changes for organisations that hold data. Keywords: artificial intelligence; training data; data governance; web crawling; robots.txt; data licensing; platform labour; privacy; copyright; synthetic data Use of AI: this paper was prepared with generative AI tools, which compiled and analysed the open datasets and drafted the text. The author takes responsibility for its content. Competing interests: the author is CEO of AIData.Broker, which acts for companies that license their data to AI developers and publishes the open datasets the paper draws on. items.title: How Perceived AI-Driven Personalization Is Associated with Online Purchase Intention in Tourism E-Commerce: A Moderated Sequential Mediation Model of Perceived Relevance and Trust in AI Recommendations
items.abstract: This study examines how perceived artificial intelligence (AI)-driven personalization is associated with online purchase intention in tourism e-commerce. It develops a moderated sequential mediation model in which perceived recommendation relevance and trust in AI recommendations represent distinct evaluative pathways, while perceived AI response creativity and AI recommendation transparency condition different relationships within the proposed model. Data were collected from 871 consumers with recent experience using personalized recommendations on AI-enabled tourism platforms or travel assistants. Respondents were recruited through experience-based purposive sampling and screened to ensure direct and recallable experience with AI-generated travel recommendations. The proposed relationships were examined using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Perceived AI-driven personalization was positively associated with perceived recommendation relevance, trust in AI recommendations, and online purchase intention. Perceived recommendation relevance and trust in AI recommendations were also positively associated with online purchase intention, while perceived recommendation relevance was positively related to trust in AI recommendations. Both constructs showed significant separate indirect associations between perceived AI-driven personalization and online purchase intention, and the theoretically ordered sequential indirect pathway was also statistically supported. Because the direct association remained significant and operated in the same direction as the indirect pathways, the observed statistical pattern was consistent with complementary partial mediation rather than evidence of a causal mediation mechanism. Perceived AI response creativity positively moderated the association between perceived AI-driven personalization and perceived recommendation relevance, whereas AI recommendation transparency positively moderated the association between perceived recommendation relevance and trust in AI recommendations. The study distinguishes perceived AI-driven personalization from perceived recommendation relevance by treating the former as consumers’ assessment of adaptive recommendation tailoring and the latter as their judgment of recommendation–decision fit. It further conceptualizes perceived recommendation relevance and trust in AI recommendations as distinct organism evaluations reflecting cognitive fit and reliance-oriented judgment, respectively. Creativity and transparency are positioned as relationship-specific boundary conditions rather than temporal stages, providing a more differentiated account of the theoretically ordered statistical pathways linking perceived AI-driven personalization with online purchase intention in tourism e-commerce.

items.title: Indistinguishable Agents: Training Agent Privacy as Twin-World Indistinguishability
items.abstract: LLM agents search, shop and send messages for their users, and every action is seen by some party. Existing privacy training rewards agents for not mentioning protected items, yet an observer can infer a private fact from what the agent does. Since an observer learns a fact only if its view changes with the fact, we propose \methodfull (\method), which trains on twin worlds that differ only in the private fact. A frozen distinguisher scores each observer's view by its log-likelihood ratio for the true world, and paired GRPO trains the agent on task success minus this ratio. We prove that this objective controls the Bayes success of every observer on every channel. On shopping and messaging tasks \method removes the leakage that disclosure judges and query-level rewards miss, while the agent still completes its tasks.

items.title: Infinite Players: Self-Improving AI Agents In Video Games That Learn, Adapt, Remember, and Evolve Beyond Human Expertise - AERÍN Continuation Algebra, Revisable Evidence, and Semantic-Trajectory Preservation
items.abstract: Infinite Players develops AERÍN Continuation Algebra, a mathematical and executable research framework connecting game-agent improvement, behavioral preservation, temporal inference, revisable memory, and statistical validation. Its central question is precise: how can an artificial descendant become more effective while preserving the behavioral process specified by its source? The framework treats preservation as an explicit mathematical contract. It distinguishes the behavior that must remain invariant from the execution details that may improve, and distinguishes an agent’s current interpretation of its source from the evidence required to revise that interpretation later. This release supplies finite-model theorems, runnable Python implementations, synthetic experiments, exact small-instance audits, and a demonstration connecting source evidence to an improved executor. The broader title expresses the long-term research direction; the verified results concern finite, known-model systems. The central preservation problem Matching a player’s immediate action preferences does not necessarily preserve the course of a session. Different motor actions can produce different subsequent situations, even when they belong to the same tactical category. An agent may therefore retain local action-class preferences while progressively changing the distribution of encounters, transitions, and future decisions. AERÍN addresses this by protecting the joint distribution of the next semantic action and the next semantic state. This transition-level contract accounts for how present execution changes future situations. It provides a foundation for separating compatible performance improvement from behavioral drift. Mathematical and computational contributions Semantic-trajectory preservation through constrained policy fibers For each ground state, the framework constructs a transition-signature matrix describing how available motor actions contribute to semantic actions and subsequent semantic states. A target semantic kernel determines a convex set of admissible action distributions, called a policy fiber. Under correct dynamics, fixed semantic maps, a shared initial semantic distribution, and realizable targets, every executor remaining inside these fibers generates the same declared semantic trajectory law at every finite horizon. The result permits history-dependent action selection and adaptive internal controller revisions, provided that the executed distributions continue to satisfy the contract. Preservation concerns the specified semantic process. Motor realization, ground-state details, and other excluded quantities may differ. Compatible policy improvement and an explicit no-headroom criterion The control layer projects exact action values into the nullspace of the transition-signature matrix. From an interior feasible policy, a controlled step along this direction preserves the semantic constraints while producing nonnegative Bellman advantage. The framework also identifies a stopping boundary: for an interior feasible policy, vanishing projected action values at every state characterize optimality under the same preservation contract. Boundary policies require the corresponding feasibility or linear-programming treatment. Constrained policy iteration with linear-programming subproblems supplies a stronger optimization reference and records numerical feasibility and duality checks. This separates the existence of compatible improvement from the effectiveness of a particular update procedure. Future-calibration memory requirements The memory analysis distinguishes a compact present answer from an archive sufficient for future reinterpretation. A finite construction shows that an unknown identity containing only one bit can nevertheless require retaining an n-bit source record when every later coordinate-specific calibration must be answered exactly. The requirement arises from preserving relationships between the identity and possible future observations. It does not imply that the identity itself contains n bits. A lossy extension yields the lower bound b ≥ n[1 − h₂(ε)], relating retained memory to average recovery error under the stated query model. The result makes the future-query contract an explicit part of memory design. Exact source-indexed revision with ordered evidence operators A balanced operator tree preserves fixed-catalog hidden Markov sequence likelihoods. Revising an existing source interpretation replaces its corresponding factor and recomputes the affected ancestors, producing the same likelihood as corrected full replay. For n events, H hypotheses, and K hidden states, dense construction costs O(nHK³), a local revision costs O(HK³ log n), and retained operator payload requires O(nHK²) storage. Full vector-forward replay costs O(nHK²) per sequence evaluation. The mechanism targets repeated sparse corrections after compilation. Its preprocessing and storage costs are disclosed explicitly; it does not provide a universal compression advantage. Coupled uncertainty and persistent latent continuation The framework retains dependencies between source identity and unresolved world properties when those dependencies affect future behavior. A latent branch is selected persistently for continuation, rather than independently resampled before every action. The accompanying composition analysis connects evidence approximation to semantic execution error under explicit shared-model assumptions. Approximation certificates require their stated support and perturbation conditions. Generated alternatives can inform proposals, but do not become additional independent source observations. Calibration-dependent improvement freedom Genuine mechanics measurements can eliminate incompatible world hypotheses and relax constraints on admissible execution. This can enlarge the feasible policy fiber. A larger fiber, however, need not contain a useful reward direction. The release includes both a positive calibration example and a negative control, separating reduced constraint rank from demonstrated performance gain. Lifetime false-promotion budgets Successive candidate versions receive fresh, bounded-gain audits with a summable allocation of statistical error. Under the stated conditional-independence and fixed-audit assumptions, this controls the probability of ever falsely promoting a candidate across repeated evaluations. The guarantee concerns acceptance errors. The existence of useful proposals, reliable improvement detection, and sustained improvement of the learning procedure remain separate research questions. Executed results The main control experiment uses an original six-state stochastic tactical environment with known dynamics and 16 seeded instances. Mean normalized discounted value increases from 0.511568 for the source anchor to 0.642583 for the path-preserving LP optimum. The paired gain is 0.131014, with a descriptive 95% interval of [0.116649, 0.145380]. Mean total variation between the exactly enumerated six-step semantic trajectory distributions is 4.30 × 10⁻¹⁶. Controllers operating under weaker preservation constraints obtain higher returns alongside substantial semantic drift. These comparisons expose the reward–preservation tradeoff rather than treating differently constrained objectives as interchangeable. In the sequence-inference experiments, the operator tree agrees with an independently implemented full-HMM replay to a maximum posterior discrepancy of 5.33 × 10⁻¹⁵ across 3,000 short synthetic records. With 32 events and a genuine simulated-world calibration, both exact methods correctly classify 999 of 1,000 synthetic binary types. The tree reorganizes inference and revision; it does not improve the statistical accuracy of the same exact Bayesian model. Additional studies examine temporal dependence, retrospective memory budgets, approximation certificates, calibration-induced changes in control freedom, local revision costs, and repeated promotion audits. Executable evidence-to-agent demonstration The supplied demonstration connects the principal components: Generate a synthetic source recording with explicit event identities and timing. Infer a coupled posterior over source and world hypotheses. Apply a genuine measurement from the simulated world. Select a persistent latent source branch. Optimize an executor satisfying the protected semantic kernel. Execute a stochastic trajectory. Export a player capsule containing the source digest, uncertainty, source and descendant policies, preservation contract, exclusions, and numerical audit scope. This makes the relationships between evidence, interpretation, improvement, execution, and exported guarantees inspectable in one finite pipeline. Contents and reproducibility The release includes a 49-page manuscript, editable LaTeX sources, seven figures, runnable Python modules, the original tactical simulator, synthetic result and trial tables, exact arithmetic audits, a ten-family proof-to-code claim ledger, reproduction scripts, reference hashes, and detailed documentation. Fresh preparation-time execution passed 50/50 v3 tests (100%) and matched 32/32 deterministic reference files (100%). These percentages describe the supplied verification checks. They do not measure completion of real-player reconstruction or general recursive self-improvement. The original v2 archive was separately reproduced, passing 22/22 tests and matching 14/14 original hashes. Those legacy results are distinguished from the v3 findings; the nested legacy archive is omitted from the focused distribution. Windows and portable Python upload utilities are included as distribution conveniences. Research scope and status The completed contribution is a finite mathematical and computational research release. items.title: It's Complicated: Factors Influencing the Effectiveness of LLM-Generated Feedback in a Live Programming Course
items.abstract: We report on three iterations of an LLM-generated feedback system deployed in a live web development course, spanning three underlying models and three feedback formats. We ask how feedback presence and its characteristics (length, complexity, format) relate to student performance, whether prior feedback exposure is associated with final-project performance, and how performance changes after first exposure. Feedback was associated with more favorable immediate outcomes in several comparisons, but the pattern varied by outcome and period. In pooled models, longer feedback was associated with lower next-submission correctness, more remaining attempts, and longer resubmission time. Prior same-part feedback was associated with lower final-project solve probability. Student-level comparisons found differences on final-project steps begun before exposure, while within-student changes across steps were uncertain. These comparisons do not identify the causal effect of feedback. Changes on standard exercises were more favorable among exposed students, but the groups' different course-stage splits limit causal interpretation. Bounded message length and student choice of format are directions for experimental evaluation. Our final-project analysis captures follow-up performance rather than directly measuring learning or understanding.

items.title: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence for Emotional Intelligence Management in Public Universities: Antidote for Improving Lecturers' Well-being in Lagos State, Nigeria
items.abstract: This study explored the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as an antidote for improving lecturers' well-being through effective emotional intelligence management in public universities in Lagos State, Nigeria. The emotional well-being of lecturers has become a critical concern in public universities due to increasing workloads, overcrowded classroom, technological disruptions, and the pressure to achieve excellence in teaching, research, and community service. The study adopted a conceptual approach and explores how AI-powered tools such as intelligent counselling systems, emotion recognition software, virtual assistants, and predictive analytics can assist lecturers in monitoring emotions, managing stress, enhancing interpersonal relationships, and maintaining psychological balance. The study further argues that integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) with emotional intelligence competencies can foster resilience, job satisfaction, motivation, and a positive work environment among academic staff. In addition, issues relating to digital literacy, ethical considerations, institutional support, and data privacy are discussed as essential factors for successful implementation. The study concludes that the strategic deployment of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for emotional intelligence management offers a sustainable solution for enhancing lecturers' well-being and overall institutional effectiveness. It is therefore recommended that university administrators should invest in AI-driven emotional support systems and develop policies that encourage responsible and inclusive AI adoption in Nigerian public universities. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Emotional Intelligence Management, Lecturers' Well-being, and Public Universities.

items.title: Mapping University Students Risk of Dependence on Generative Artificial Intelligence Using K-Means Clustering
items.abstract: The growing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has changed how university students approach academic tasks. Although these tools can support learning and improve efficiency, frequent reliance on them raises concerns about students' ability to study and solve problems independently. This study aims to identify patterns of GenAI use among university students and explore potential indicators of dependence through K-Means clustering. An exploratory quantitative approach was adopted, using questionnaire responses collected through 15 items measured on a five-point Likert scale. Of the 106 responses received, 104 met the inclusion criteria and were retained for analysis. The data underwent screening, numerical encoding, and reverse scoring before being grouped using the K-Means algorithm. The appropriate number of clusters was selected by comparing Silhouette Scores across solutions containing two to seven clusters. The analysis identified three student groups, with a Silhouette Score of 0.2443. The first group comprised 30 students (28.85%) who showed relatively higher GenAI use and stronger indications of behavioral dependence. The second group included 11 students (10.58%) who reported lower GenAI use but demonstrated limitations in academic independence and understanding. The remaining 63 students (60.58%) formed a group characterized by moderate GenAI use. These findings suggest that frequency of use alone does not adequately reflect the risk of dependence. However, the relatively low Silhouette Score indicates limited separation between groups, meaning that the resulting profiles should be interpreted as exploratory rather than definitive.

items.title: Mental Workload: Physiological Assessment and Validation Using Visual Stimuli
items.abstract: ABSTRACT This paper provides a notion for the use of electroencephalography (EEG) in the field of cognitive science. In particular, we investigated the brain activity of operators while spotting the differences in similar‐looking pictures at three levels of difficulty. As many practical loads are fundamentally intrinsic, the task was designed to specifically induce intrinsic workload (the productive load as per Cognitive Load Theory (CLT)). The experiment used the task: Spot the Difference to create a workload scenario comprising three difficulty levels: spotting five differences, three more differences, and two more differences (along with retaining the previous differences from working memory). The task was designed intrinsically as the operators are generally occupied with tasks involving working memory and requiring attention towards the varying number of resources. By utilising the brain signatures a mental workload model was developed employing a Support Vector Machine (SVM) as the classifier. The workload levels were classified within an accuracy range of 84% to 98% ( p < 0.05). Moreover, using subjective ratings about the workload on NASA's Task Load Index (NASA‐TLX) rating scale, workload scores were obtained for validation corresponding to the difficulty levels. Finally, a correlation study showed the association of different EEG features with the workload score within a correlation coefficient range of 0.306 to 0.748 ( p < 0.05 2‐tailed). The reported results can also provide new insights into the cognitive workload assessment of the operators at various phases of task loads. Findings of this type may lead to the industrial and professional measurement and improvement of cognitive aptitude soon.

items.title: On the ROAD™ to Transparent AI Disclosure in Research
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities continue to advance, and researchers increasingly use AI to help them reach their research goals. As a result, disclosing AI use has become essential. Yet researchers face a dilemma about whether to disclose how they used AI. Disclosure may reduce others' trust in their findings, while hiding AI use risks later discovery and damage to their reputation. I argue that researchers should disclose, and that effective disclosure begins with keeping a thorough record of their AI use, which I call an AI research footprint. I then introduce the ROAD™ framework (Request, Output, Assess, Decide), which helps researchers report what they asked AI to do, what it produced, how they assessed the output, and what they decided.

items.title: Optimizing Agentic Artificial Intelligence to Improve Business Process Automation Efficiency through Modern Digital Technology
items.abstract: In the era of digital transformation, traditional Business Process Automation (BPA) still faces limitations in handling dynamic, unstructured, and complex decision-making tasks. Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI), which is characterized by autonomous agents capable of advanced reasoning, dynamic planning, and multi-step workflow execution, is considered a promising approach to improving the efficiency and adaptability of enterprise operations. This study aims to examine how Agentic AI can be optimized to improve BPA performance within modern digital ecosystems. Using a qualitative approach through a literature study, this paper synthesizes recent academic literature, theoretical models, and technological frameworks related to intelligent automation. The review indicates that integrating Agentic AI into enterprise business architectures has the potential to move beyond rigid, rule-based automation by enabling adaptive problem-solving, real-time context awareness, and cross-system collaboration. The reviewed literature also suggests that autonomous agents may help reduce operational bottlenecks, lower human intervention in routine cognitive workflows, and support more efficient resource allocation across organizational functions. In addition, this study identifies key implementation challenges, including system interoperability, algorithmic transparency, data privacy risks, and the governance mechanisms required for secure deployment. This study contributes to the literature on enterprise automation by proposing strategic considerations for organizations that seek to use digital technology to build more resilient, scalable, and intelligent business processes. Because this is a literature-based study, the findings are conceptual and do not provide empirical evidence of efficiency gains.

items.title: PERSISTENT HOMOLOGY ON LOCAL EXPLANATION SPACES: A TOPOLOGICAL FRAMEWORK FOR EXPLAINABLE AI IN DECISION SUPPORT SYSTEMS
items.abstract: We propose a novel framework that re-architects explainable artificial intelligence within decision support systems by integrating persistent homology into the explanation pipeline. Conventional approaches treat local feature attributions, such as SHAP values, as isolated scalar values for individual predictions, thereby overlooking the multi-scale interaction structures that emerge across a dataset. To address this limitation, we embed a collection of local explanation vectors into a metric space and compute persistent homology using the Vietoris-Rips complex. This topological analysis yields a set of persistence diagrams that capture the birth and death of homology generators across multiple scales. From these diagrams, we construct a global interaction tensor that encodes the total persistence of topological features involving pairs of input features. This tensor is then incorporated into the decision support system’s utility model as a regularization term, which penalizes or rewards the co-occurrence of high-magnitude attributions on features that persistently interact across the dataset. The resulting system provides decision-makers with queryable, multi-scale explanations at selectable persistence thresholds, transforming the interface from a static explainer into a dynamic topological reasoning tool. For instance, a user can request all feature pairs with persistence above a given threshold in a specific homology dimension, and the system highlights those interactions in the explanation. The proposed method is realized using the Ripser algorithm for efficient computation on datasets of up to one hundred thousand instances, with periodic updates via a streaming variant. Our contribution is a principled mathematical framework that bridges topological data analysis and explainable AI, offering a new perspective on feature interaction discovery and explanation stability. The significance lies in its ability to reveal robust, higher-order interaction structures that are invisible to standard attribution methods, thereby enhancing the interpretability and trustworthiness of model-driven decisions.

items.title: Preserving Human Judgment in AI-Enabled Education: The SAM Model for AI Readiness, Assessment, and Human-in-the-Loop Decision Making
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) shifts educational focus from access to information toward judging machine-generated claims and regulating the division of epistemic work. This conceptual article proposes the SAM model—self-regulation (S), ambiguity tolerance (A), and methodological competence (M)—as a bounded person-level resource model within broader AI readiness, with educators’ AI readiness as a central application. S denotes regulatory capacity, A a disposition-like willingness to tolerate unresolved epistemic ambiguity, and M the capacity to evaluate claims, differentiated into cross-domain M1 and domain-specific M2. SAM’s distinctive claim is configurational: M should predict independently assessed judgment more strongly at higher S and, under high ambiguity, when A is higher. These relations, the M1/M2 distinction, limited compensability, and incremental prediction beyond shared and neighboring accounts remain hypothetical. The model separates resources from enacted processes, contextual affordances, and outcomes and requires independent performance criteria. For AI-based assessment and learning analytics, educators’ interpretations of AI-derived evidence and construct inferences from behavioral traces require validated mappings addressing alternative explanations, comparability, fairness, and use. SAM thus offers a research agenda predicting when AI support preserves human judgment rather than merely improving supported performance.

items.title: Prevalence and correlates of GenerativeAI chatbot use for mental health concerns in higher education students
items.abstract: Background Large language model chatbots are increasingly used for mental health help-seeking, with general-purpose systems like ChatGPT becoming popular among young adults despite concerns about accuracy and misinformation. High rates of mental distress in higher education attending emerging adults make them an important focal population to characterize and contextual the use of generativeAI models for mental health in. Methods Data were collected from the 2024-2025 Healthy Minds Study at a large, public 4-year university. Of 12,000 students invited, 2071 participated; 896 bachelor-level students aged 18–24 years were randomly selected to complete a module with generativeAI questions, and 809 (90.2%) had complete data. Measures included chatbot use for mental health support, perceived AI trustworthiness, AI knowledge, mental health diagnosis, perceived need for help, past-year mental health treatment, barriers to care, other forms of informal help-seeking, and demographics. Weighted logistic regression models examined associations between these variables and chatbot use for mental health support. Results 15.4% of students reported using generalized chatbots for mental health help-seeking. Significant correlates included greater perceived need for help, experiencing more barriers to clinical care use, higher perceived trust in AI for mental health information, lower AI knowledge, and identifying as Asian. Specific barriers of financial constraints, limited time, fear of clinician mistreatment due to identity and privacy concerns were linked to chatbot usage. Conclusions GenerativeAI chatbots are a notable source of mental health support for college students, especially among those facing access barriers and who perceive AI as trustworthy. Future initiatives should educate young adults about chatbot capabilities and limitations and promote equitable mental health support.

items.title: Prompt‐based emotional scaffolding in generative AI : Effects on self‐regulated learning and socio‐emotional outcomes
items.abstract: Abstract While generative AI (GenAI) tools are emerging as educational resources, general‐purpose applications like ChatGPT are not explicitly designed to support the metacognitive and socio‐emotional dimensions of learning, often failing to address students' emotional states or promote independent thinking. In response, this study introduces a CVT‐SRL GenAI Support Framework integrating control‐value theory (CVT) and self‐regulated learning (SRL) and tests a learner‐centred GenAI chatbot design employing prompt‐based SRL scaffolding and emotional support. In a preregistered experiment in an authentic educational setting, 144 high school students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) ChatGPT, (2) SRLbot (GenAI with SRL scaffolding), (3) emotional SRLbot (GenAI with SRL and emotional support). Outcomes included conceptual knowledge and transfer, trace‐based and self‐reported engagement in SRL phases (forethought, performance, self‐reflection), enjoyment, boredom, hopelessness, self‐efficacy and trust. Data were collected at pretest, posttest and 4‐week follow‐up. Across conditions, students showed improvements in conceptual knowledge and transfer from pretest to posttest, with no significant condition differences in post‐to‐follow‐up change. Both SRLbot and Emotional SRLbot were associated with higher self‐reported enjoyment and lower boredom than ChatGPT and elicited trace‐based SRL behaviours. Moreover, Emotional SRLbot prompted greater engagement in performance‐phase and self‐reflection processes than the other conditions. These findings provide preliminary evidence that GenAI agents integrating SRL and emotional scaffolding can support more positive emotional states and task‐level SRL behaviours than general‐purpose GenAI, highlighting control‐value appraisals as a promising target for emotionally supportive SRL design. Future research should explore longitudinal effects on SRL skill development and independent regulation. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT have shown promise in enhancing learning outcomes, but they also present challenges in supporting socio‐emotional needs, fostering metacognition and promoting higher‐order thinking. Applying self‐regulated learning (SRL) frameworks in chatbot‐assisted learning has been found to foster learner autonomy, long‐term engagement and improved learning outcomes. Achievement emotions experienced during learning play a critical role in supporting self‐regulated learning, motivation and academic achievement. Interventions that target learners' perceptions of control and value through reappraisal can effectively foster positive emotions. What this paper adds An investigation of the impact of three GenAI conversational agents (standard ChatGPT, an SRL agent and an emotionally supportive SRL agent) on cognitive and socio‐emotional outcomes as well as task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours among high school students in an authentic classroom setting. Preliminary evidence that integrating prompts which target self‐regulated learning phases and learners' emotional states, as well as address perceptions of control and value can increase students' enjoyment of concrete learning situations and reduce boredom more effectively than standard ChatGPT. Insights into how theoretically grounded GenAI agents that incorporate SRL and emotional scaffolding may support students' emotional engagement and task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours during a short classroom learning activity. Implications for practice and/or policy Prompt engineering can be used to simulate emotional support and personalize guidance based on SRL and emotion regulation principles, providing design considerations for future learner‐centred GenAI systems. Developers and educators aiming to design pedagogically meaningful GenAI tools should focus on scaffolding SRL both cognitively and emotionally, to support the affective and self‐regulatory dimensions of learning. We make the technical specifications and system prompts publicly available.

items.title: Psychological correlates of dependence on generative and conversational AI: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Background. Dependence on generative and conversational artificial intelligence (AI) is measured with diverse instruments spanning addiction criteria, task reliance, and emotional bonding. No meta-analysis has pooled its psychological correlates across populations. Methods. We conducted a pre-registered three-level meta-analysis (Zenodo: 10.5281/zenodo.23420672) searching eight electronic databases and citations of instrument papers on 16 October 2026, with citation chasing. Zero-order correlations were pooled using correlated and hierarchical effects models on Fisher's z with cluster-robust inference (CR2). Scale type (T1 addiction-type, T2 functional, T3 emotional, T4 mixed) was the primary moderator. Certainty was rated via GRADE. Results. We included 127 samples (123 studies; N = 74,492; 29 countries; 70% university students; 39% mainland China). AI dependence correlated moderately with anxiety (r = 0.37, 95% CI [0.25, 0.48]), stress (r = 0.35 [0.25, 0.43]), depression (r = 0.32 [0.21, 0.42]), social anxiety (r = 0.36 [0.17, 0.53]), loneliness (r = 0.28 [0.18, 0.38]), and procrastination (r = 0.26 [0.12, 0.40]), and weakly and inversely with self-esteem (r = −0.18 [−0.35, −0.00]). All 95% prediction intervals crossed zero. Addiction-type and mixed scales showed no detectable difference; functional and emotional scales were rarely paired with clinical outcomes. Certainty was low to very low. Conclusions. AI dependence moderately correlates with distress and self-regulation difficulties, but prediction intervals cross zero and evidence certainty is low. Functional and emotional dependence have rarely been studied alongside clinical outcomes.

items.title: Registered Nurses' Experiences of Clinical Decision‐Making: A Qualitative Descriptive Study to Inform Artificial Intelligence‐Assisted Decision Support in Nursing
items.abstract: AIM: To describe registered nurses' experiences of clinical decision-making and identify needs that may inform future development of artificial-intelligence-assisted clinical decision support systems in nursing. DESIGN: A qualitative descriptive study. METHODS: Data were collected between 2022 and 2025 through 16 semi-structured interviews with registered nurses working in inpatient wards at a Finnish university hospital. The data were analysed using inductive content analysis. RESULTS: Perceived challenges in clinical decision-making were related to organisational issues, multiprofessional collaboration, nurse-patient interactions, professional factors and availability and trustworthiness of data. The findings also identified support needs related to health information management, clinical workflows and quality of nursing care that may inform future artificial intelligence-assisted clinical decision support system development. CONCLUSION: Nurses experienced multifaceted challenges and needs in clinical decision-making, shaped by organisational, professional, relational and information-related factors. Adoption of artificial intelligence-assisted decision support systems may represent one potential approach to optimising clinical decision-making, improving patient care quality and enhancing workflow efficiency. Realising these opportunities requires coordinated efforts at individual, organisational and societal levels, including competence development, workflow redesign, strong data governance and a culture that fosters trust in technology. IMPLICATIONS FOR THE PROFESSION AND/OR PATIENT CARE: The findings may inform the future development of artificial intelligence-assisted clinical decision support systems in nursing. REPORTING METHOD: The Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research checklist was used when reporting the results. PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: Registered nurses participated in the study. IMPACT: What problem did the study address? This paper addresses existing gaps and unmet needs in nursing clinical decision-making What were the main findings? The main findings highlight several key opportunities for artificial intelligence-assisted clinical decision support systems in nursing. Where and on whom will the research have an impact? The research may inform efforts to optimise health information management, streamline clinical workflows and improve the quality of nursing care.

items.abstract: Role of Artificial Intelligence in Modern Banking Services: Benefits, Customer Experience and Challenges This research investigates the transformative role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in modern banking services, with particular emphasis on operational efficiency, customer experience, and emerging challenges. It examines the application of AI-driven technologies, including machine learning, intelligent chatbots, predictive analytics, and automated fraud detection, in streamlining banking operations, enhancing service personalisation, improving risk management, and supporting data-driven decision-making. Furthermore, the study evaluates key concerns associated with AI adoption, including data privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, transparency, and customer trust. By assessing both the benefits and limitations of AI integration, this research aims to develop a comprehensive understanding of its implications for the banking sector and highlight the importance of responsible, secure, and customer-centric AI implementation in the evolving financial services landscape.

items.title: Savoir / Action — English Translation (V1)
items.abstract: An AI agent can be given an objective by a human, then search, interpret, plan, use tools, and act before returning a result. The human remains present. But how much of this activity can they still understand, verify, or influence? Savoir / Action begins with this difficulty. The manuscript examines the relationship between the knowledge an AI agent treats as valid, the means it uses to act, and the constraints that shape its trajectory. It asks what human supervision can still mean when control cannot be reduced to permissions, a stop button, or approval of the final result. This reflection grew out of exploratory work conducted within a human–AI dyad. We have chosen to make this origin explicit because it is part of the very question we are examining. We do not claim to have established a theory. We present our thinking as it stands: some distinctions have become clearer, some questions remain open, and several propositions still need to be challenged by other perspectives. This is the canonical English translation of the original French manuscript, first published on 5 October 2026: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23164286

items.title: Synthetic corroboration: when AI interpretation looks like independent evidence
items.abstract: People increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (AI) to interpret the motives, emotions, and likely actions of absent others. This article develops synthetic corroboration, defined as the inflation of perceived independent target-specific evidential support when an externally attributed AI interpretation remains substantially dependent on evidence supplied by the user. The construct distinguishes independence of target-specific source access and information from analytical independence: AI may contribute general knowledge, alternative hypotheses, or inferential processing without providing an independent evidential source. Drawing on research on interpersonal inference, advice taking, source dependence, judgement aggregation, source monitoring, machine agency, and social sycophancy, the article proposes a programme of discriminating tests. The core experiment crosses source attribution with structural transformation while holding target-specific evidence constant, comparing AI with self-reformulation and a human adviser given the same evidence. The central prediction is that transformation will disproportionately increase perceived evidential independence under AI attribution and reduce subsequent acquisition of genuinely independent information. AI–human equivalence, failure to predict information seeking, or reduction to established constructs would narrow or defeat the AI-specific account.n psychological fluency or agreement.
